title: 1099-NEC threshold at $2,000: Run the Vendor Payment Test Across Every Client From the Books Before FIRE Closes November 19
excerpt: The IRS has posted the December 2026 revision of the 1099-NEC and 1099-MISC instructions with the $2,000 1099-NEC threshold for 2026 payments, updated its Form 1099-K page on October 28, 2026, and set November 19 as the last day to file through FIRE. Here is how an accounting firm runs the vendor payment test from the ledger across every client now: calendar-year cash by vendor and paying account, card and app payments out, corporations out except legal services, and a per-client tie-out to the general ledger.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Accounting firm staff running the 2026 1099-NEC threshold vendor payment test across client QuickBooks files with a W-9 folder and the IRS instructions open
content:
The 1099-NEC threshold for payments made in 2026 is $2,000 per payee, up from $600, and it is tested on cash paid during the calendar year, not on expense booked. Card and payment app payments are excluded because the processor reports them on Form 1099-K. Run that test for every client from the ledger now.

Why this matters now

Three IRS dates line up in the next three weeks. On 2026-10-28 the IRS updated its Understanding your Form 1099-K page, which states that payment apps and online marketplaces report payments on Form 1099-K when the total for goods or services exceeds $20,000 in more than 200 transactions. That is the form that catches card and app payments, so it is the reason those payments come out of a client's 1099-NEC test.

The December 2026 revision of the Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC is already posted on irs.gov. It says that for tax years beginning after 2025 the minimum threshold for reporting certain payments, and for backup withholding on those payments, increased to $2,000, and may be adjusted for inflation beginning in calendar year 2027. The same instructions keep the $10 royalty threshold, the $600 threshold for gross proceeds paid to an attorney, and the $5,000 direct sales threshold. So the test is not one number. It is one number for most boxes and three exceptions.

The filing system is changing at the same time. IRS news release IR-2026-99, dated 2026-08-24, reminded filers that FIRE is being retired. November 9, 2026 is the deadline to modify a transmitter control code application, and November 19, 2026 at 3 p.m. Eastern is the last day to submit information returns through FIRE. Tax year 2026 returns go through IRIS in the 2027 filing season, and a firm that does not hold an IRIS transmitter control code yet needs to apply before it needs to file. Payroll and tax coverage published this week, such as OnPay's November 2 explainer, walks through the new amounts. What it does not do is show a firm how to run the test across forty client files from the ledger, which is the part that takes the hours.

What the $2,000 threshold changes and what it leaves alone

A self-contained definition first. The 1099-NEC threshold is the minimum total of reportable payments a single payer must have made to a single payee during a calendar year before the payer must file Form 1099-NEC for that payee. For payments made in 2026 the amount is $2,000. Reportable means paid for services by a non-employee, by a method other than a payment card or third-party network, to a payee that is not a corporation, with an exception for legal services.

Form and boxPayments made in 2025Payments made in 2026What lands here
1099-NEC box 1, nonemployee compensation$600$2,000Contractors, freelancers, legal fees for services
1099-MISC box 1, rents$600$2,000Rent paid to an individual or partnership landlord
1099-MISC box 3, other income$600$2,000Prizes, awards, settlements
1099-MISC box 2, royalties$10$10Unchanged
1099-MISC box 10, gross proceeds paid to an attorney$600$600Unchanged
1099-MISC box 7, direct sales$5,000$5,000Unchanged
1099-K, filed by the processorNot your client's form$20,000 and more than 200 transactionsCard and payment app payments
Backup withholding trigger$600$2,000Reportable payee with no TIN on file

Four things did not change. The test is cash basis: a bill dated December 2025 and paid in January 2026 counts in 2026. The test is per payer: two client entities with separate employer identification numbers that each paid the same contractor are two separate tests, and the group total is irrelevant. Payments to corporations stay exempt, except for legal services. And the due date holds: Form 1099-NEC is due to the recipient and the IRS by January 31, which in 2027 falls on a Sunday, so the practical date is Monday, February 1, 2027. Form 1099-MISC follows at the end of February on paper or March 31 electronically.

One thing is new and easy to miss. The $2,000 floor also applies to backup withholding, so a vendor who never returned a W-9 and was paid $1,500 by check this year does not trigger withholding, while one paid $2,500 does. That is why November is the month to chase W-9s, while the vendor still wants the December payment.

The vendor payment test, one firm's November worked through

Call the firm Harbor Books: forty-two QuickBooks Online clients, two staff accountants on 1099 duty, and a partner who signs off. The figures are illustrative. In past years the firm pulled a 1099 transaction detail report per client in January, fixed the vendor flags it found, and filed by the end of the month. This year the test runs in November, from the ledger, in four steps per client.

Step one: every vendor's calendar-year cash, by payment method

The query is the same for every client: all payments dated January 1 through today, grouped by vendor, with the bank or credit card account the payment cleared from. Bill payments, checks, and expenses all count. Journal entries that credit cash and debit an expense count too, and they are the ones the vendor flag report misses. Split the total into two columns: paid from a bank account, and paid by credit card or through a payment app. Only the first column is tested.

Step two: the threshold test with the exceptions

Take one client, a landscaping company. Vendor A, a sole proprietor doing subcontract work, was paid $2,400 this year: $1,500 by check and $900 on the company card. The $900 on the card is the processor's job on Form 1099-K. The testable amount is $1,500, under the 1099-NEC threshold, so no form unless December pushes the check total to $2,000 or more. Vendor B, the office landlord, an individual, was paid $1,950 in rent through October with November and December still to pay. At $2,340 by year end she crosses the rent threshold and gets a 1099-MISC. Vendor C, a law firm organized as a corporation, was paid $3,100 for contract review. Corporations are exempt except for legal services, so Vendor C gets a 1099-NEC. Vendor D, an equipment lessor paid $8,000, is a corporation and gets nothing.

Step three: the projection

A test run in November is a projection, not the filing figure. For every vendor between $1,200 and $2,000 in the bank column, add the open bills and the usual December run rate and flag the ones that will cross. Those are the vendors whose W-9 the firm requests this week. Harbor Books found 61 such vendors across its 42 clients, 19 of them with no W-9 on file.

Step four: the January rerun and the tie-out

In the first week of January the same query runs again over the full year, and the result is the filing figure. The tie-out is one line per client: testable payments to vendors at or over the threshold, plus testable payments to vendors under it, plus card and app payments, plus payments to exempt corporations, equals total cash paid to vendors for the year per the general ledger. If it does not, a payment is miscoded, and the gap says how big. The firm's FIRE to IRIS reconciliation covers what happens after that figure is final. The per-vendor view it starts from is the one described in the vendor spend analysis guide.

The workload changes shape more than size. Under the old $600 floor Harbor Books filed about 1,100 forms. Under $2,000 it expects about 640. The hours do not fall in proportion, because the exception vendors and the W-9 chase are the same work at either floor. What moves is the timing: the January crunch becomes a November review, where there is time to do it right.

Accounting controls for the 1099-NEC threshold test

Source data: the cash disbursement detail for each client for the calendar year, by vendor, with the paying account on every line (bank, credit card, or payment app clearing account); the vendor master with tax identification number, entity type, and the W-9 date; the 1099 tracking flag as currently set; and the IRS thresholds from the December 2026 instructions, kept as a dated table the firm maintains once.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Sum payments dated within the calendar year by vendor. Payments are credits to cash and debits to expense, prepaid, fixed assets, or accounts payable, and the test follows the cash credit, not the debit, so a payment booked to a balance sheet account still counts. The test is a flow for the year; the accounts payable balance at December 31 is a point-in-time figure and never enters it. Remove the lines whose credit side is a card or payment app account. Remove payees whose entity type is a corporation, unless the payment was for legal services. Compare the remainder with the threshold for the box the payment belongs to: $2,000 for nonemployee compensation, rents, and other income; $10 for royalties; $600 for attorney gross proceeds. Payees at or over the line get a form.

Review: a second person reruns one client from the raw disbursement detail and lands on the same vendor list; the per-client tie-out to total vendor cash agrees to the general ledger; every vendor over the line has a W-9 on file or a backup withholding note; every vendor flagged last year but not this year has a reason, whether threshold, payment method, or entity type; and every journal entry that credits a bank account has been assigned to a vendor or carries a written reason not to be.

Decision: the partner owns the threshold table and the exception rules and changes them once a year, when the IRS instructions change. The staff accountant owns the vendor master and the W-9 chase per client. The client owns the answer to the one question the books cannot settle: whether a vendor paid through a personal card or app was paid for the business, and whether that vendor is a corporation. The firm's bulk payee edit verification applies whenever vendor names get merged during cleanup, because a merged vendor changes the test total.

Limits and common mistakes

The threshold is tested per payer and per payee. A vendor paid $1,800 by one client entity and $1,700 by its sister entity gets no form from either, even though the group paid $3,500. Consolidated reporting is the wrong lens for this test; the firm runs it entity by entity and then looks at the group view for context.

The test is cash basis even for accrual clients. December bills paid in January belong to next year's test, and the December accrual does not matter.

Card payments come out only when they cleared through a card or a payment app. A vendor paid by ACH from the bank account is a bank payment. A vendor paid through a bill pay service that debits the client's bank account is usually a bank payment too, but some services settle through a card network, and the service's own documentation says which. Keep that answer on file per service.

Harbor Books is illustrative. The thresholds in this article are for payments made in 2026, from the December 2026 instructions, and the IRS has said they may be adjusted for inflation from 2027, so next year's table will differ.

The $2,000 floor reduces forms, not diligence. A contractor paid $1,900 in checks is still an expense the client deducts, still needs a real invoice from a real vendor, and still belongs in the vendor spend review. Fewer forms is a filing fact, not a bookkeeping one.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 1099-NEC threshold for 2026?

For payments made in 2026, a business files Form 1099-NEC for each non-employee it paid at least $2,000 for services during the calendar year, up from $600 in prior years. The IRS instructions say the amount may be adjusted for inflation beginning in 2027. Royalties keep a $10 threshold and gross proceeds paid to an attorney keep a $600 threshold on Form 1099-MISC.

Do credit card and PayPal payments count toward the $2,000?

No. Payments made with a credit card, debit card, or through a third-party payment network are reported by the payment processor on Form 1099-K and are not reported on Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC. Only payments by check, ACH, cash, or other direct methods from the client's bank account count toward the threshold.

Is the threshold tested per entity or across a group of related companies?

Per payer. Each entity with its own employer identification number tests its own payments to each vendor. Two related entities that each paid a contractor less than $2,000 file nothing, even if the combined amount exceeds $2,000. Firms that consolidate clients for management reporting need to run the 1099 test at the entity level.

When are 2026 Forms 1099-NEC due?

Form 1099-NEC is due to both the recipient and the IRS by January 31. Because January 31, 2027 falls on a Sunday, the practical deadline is Monday, February 1, 2027. Form 1099-MISC is due to the IRS by the end of February on paper or by March 31, 2027 if filed electronically.

Why does the FIRE shutdown matter for 2026 forms?

The IRS is retiring the FIRE system and moving information return filing to IRIS. In its August 24, 2026 reminder the IRS set November 19, 2026 as the last day to submit returns through FIRE and November 9, 2026 as the deadline to modify transmitter control code applications. Tax year 2026 forms are filed through IRIS in the 2027 season, so a firm needs an IRIS transmitter control code before January.

Once the test runs from the ledger instead of from the vendor flag, it stops being a January surprise.
